Cu-Catalyzed Regioselective Silylation of Chloro-Substituted
Allenyl-Bdan
Qi Ran, Ke-Fan Wu, and Yun-He Xu*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2024, 26, 3767−3771
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A copper-catalyzed efficient regioselective silylation reaction of chloro-substituted allenyl-Bdan was developed. Under
mild reaction conditions, allenyl and propargyl silane compounds can be selectively obtained in moderate to high yields by adjusting
the bases and solvents used in the reactions. This study offers direct and efficient methods for synthesizing multifunctionalized
allenyl and propargyl silane compounds from the same initial material of chloro-substituted allenyl-Bdan.
A
llenes are recognized as stable organic compounds with
two cumulated carbon−carbon double bonds, featuring
two π orbitals perpendicular to each other (Scheme 1a).
1
This
unique structure, coupled with their substituent-loading
capability, gives them distinctive reactivity and significant
potential in organic synthesis. Among them, allenyl halides
serve as valuable building blocks in chemical synthesis as a
result of their ease of conversion into various functional
groups. Most examples discovered to date focus on
constructing carbon−carbon bonds. For instance, Sonogashira
cross-coupling and Suzuki cross-coupling of allenyl halide
compounds have been previously reported.
2
Recently,
transition-metal-catalyzed C−H propargylation has emerged
as another method. The use of bromoallenes as coupling
partners in direct C−H propargylation highlights their unique
potential as building blocks in organic synthesis.
3
Additionally,
copper-catalyzed regioselectivity substitution of allenyl halides
has been extensively documented.
4
In 1987, Caporusso et al.
reported the first copper-catalyzed alkylation of bromoallenes
for alkyne and allene preparation, albeit yielding a mixture of
both products. In 2011, Knochel and co-workers
4d
used
choroallenes to synthesize trisubstituted allene compounds.
Subsequently, Alexakis and co-workers
4e,f
selectively produced
trisubstituted allenes and tetrasubstituted propargyl com-
pounds from choroallenes using different solvents. Further-
more, C−N bond formation has been achieved. In 2005, Trost
and Stiles
4i
documented copper-catalyzed coupling of allenyl
halides with amides, carbamates, and ureas to synthesize
allenamides. Hsung’s group
4j
established a series of chiral
allenamides through stereospecific amidation of optically
enriched allenyl iodides. Despite the versatile utilities of
allenamides, very few other C−X (e.g., C−Si) bond trans-

carbon-substituted allenyl and propargyl compounds without
functional groups has been unsatisfactory. Hence, there is a
strong imperative to synthesize more active allenyl and
propargyl compounds.
5

for developing multifunctionalized allenyl and propargyl silane
compounds, we present copper-catalyzed silylation reactions of
chloro-substituted allenyl-Bdan to synthesize these versatile

Et

enhanced the yield to 86% with moderate
regioselectivity (3a/4a = 25:75; entry 7 in Table 1). Replacing
Cs

3
with MeOK improved the selectivity of products 3a
and 4a to 17:83 while achieving an 83% yield (entry 10 in
Table 1). Subsequently, a variety of solvents were assessed
(entries 11−13 in Table 1), with the addition of ethyl ether
significantly enhancing selectivity but slightly reducing the
yield (entry 13 in Table 1). Remarkably, increasing the
amounts of compound 2a and KOMe used in the reaction to
2.2 equiv led to an excellent yield and single selectivity for the
formation of product 4a (entry 14 in Table 1). The reaction
proceeded without a notable decrease in the yield when
shortening the time and reducing the catalyst (entries 15 and
16 in Table 1).
With the optimized conditions established, we proceeded to
explore the range of reactions for generating product 3.
Substrates with diverse alkyl groups were efficiently trans-
formed into respective Bdan-substituted propargylic silanes,
yielding high amounts of products with remarkable selectivity
(3a−3c; Figure 1). We were pleased to discover that the
secondary alkyl substituents exhibited compatibility with the
reaction environment (3e and 3f; Figure 1). However, the
desired product could not be synthesized when utilizing t-butyl
substituents (3d; Figure 1). Additionally, a variety of primary
alkyl-substituted substrates containing potentially reactive
functional groups were also accommodated (3g−3j; Figure
1), offering opportunities for subsequent derivatization.
Notably, compounds featuring allenyl-Bdan with reactive
moieties, like furan (3k), acetal (3l), ester (3m), and silyl
ether (3n), demonstrated compatibility with the reaction
conditions. When pinB-SiMe
2
Ph replaced pinB-SiEt
3
, product
3o was obtained at a yield of 65% with single selectivity.
Following this, we initiated an exploration into the reaction
scope for synthesizing product 4. The reaction of different
alkyl-substituted allenyl-Bdan proceeded smoothly, resulting in
the formation of the respective allenylsilanes with high yields
(4a−4c, as depicted in Figure 2). Moreover, when secondary
alkyl or tertiary alkyl-substituted allenyl-Bdan compounds were
utilized, the corresponding products were also obtained in
significant yields (4d−4f; Figure 2). Various functional groups,
including double bonds (4g), diverse halides (4h−4j), furan
(4k), acetal (4l), ester (4m), and silyl ether (4n) present in the
substrates, were well-accommodated. Regrettably, the sub-
stitution of pinB-SiMe
2
Ph with pinB-SiEt
3
prevented the
synthesis of product 4o.
To showcase the practical applicability of the products, we
conducted a series of transformative reactions involving
products 3a and 4a. Initially, a gram-scale reaction of
compound 1a was performed on a 4 mmol scale, resulting in
a 93% yield for product 3a (1.48 g) and an 85% yield for
product 4a (1.35 g) (see Scheme 2). Subsequently, product 3a
was employed for C−C bond formation reactions, specifically
Sonogashira coupling reactions using iodobenzene, yielding
product 5 at a 90% yield.
4f
Subsequently, product 4a was
combined with pinacol and sulfuric acid in tetrahydrofuran.
Without further purification, crude product 6 directly proceed
to the next step of the reaction, which mixed with
salicylaldehyde in the presence of morpholine, leading to the
isolation of corresponding homopropargylic alcohol 7 with a
yield of 70% (Scheme 3).
5b

According to prior reports and our experimental findings,
4d,6
we have put forward a feasible mechanistic pathway (Scheme
4). Initially, in methanol, the combination of pinB-SiMe
2
Ph, a
copper catalyst, and a base can form species A. Subsequently, π
complex B or D may arise from the interaction of species A
with allenyl-Bdan. Following this, an antiselective elimination
process involving π complex B or D takes place, leading to the
creation of copper(II) intermediate C or E. β-Elimination from
intermediate C or E then yields the desired product 3 or 4,
with the copper catalyst being liberated for the subsequent
catalytic cycle.
In summary, we have devised an innovative copper-catalyzed
technique for producing multifunctionalized allenyl and
propargyl silane compounds from a common initial material
of chloro-substituted allenyl-Bdan. The resulting allenyl and
propargyl silane compounds serve as versatile reagents capable
of undergoing diverse conversions to generate valuable
synthetic products.
